title: Government & Democracy · Episode 2
chapters: Gerrymandering: winning by drawing the lines
Human rights: where they come from

units.t: Government & Democracy. Episode two.
In this episode: How voting works in Australia, Gerrymandering: winning by drawing the lines and Human rights: where they come from.
Part one. How voting works in Australia.
Australia gave the world the secret ballot, makes voting compulsory, and can count your ballot in several rounds.
Here's what happens to your ballot after it drops in the box.
Compulsory since 1924.
Australia is one of a small number of democracies where voting is compulsory.
Enrolment became compulsory in 1911 and voting in 1924, first applying at the 1925 election.
Turnout at the 1922 election had fallen below 60 per cent.
Since then it has usually been around 90 per cent or more.
Strictly, the legal duty is to attend a polling place, have your name marked off, and put your ballot paper in the box.
Because the ballot is secret, nobody checks how, or whether, you filled it in.
People who don't vote without a valid reason receive a modest fine.
Supporters say compulsion gives governments a mandate from everyone.
Critics argue that voting should be a free choice.
How preferences work.
For the House of Representatives, Australia uses full preferential voting, introduced federally in 1918.
You number every box in order of preference: 1 for your favourite, 2 for your next choice, and so on.
A ballot not filled in correctly is informal and doesn't count.
To win a seat, a candidate needs more than 50 per cent of formal votes.
If nobody has this after first preferences, the candidate with the fewest votes is excluded and each of their ballots passes to the next preference marked.
This repeats until someone crosses 50 per cent.
Say A has 44 per cent, B 41 per cent and C 15 per cent.
If two-thirds of C's voters put B second, B gains 10 per cent and wins with 51 per cent.
So you can back a minor candidate without 'wasting' your vote.
Voting for the Senate.
The Senate ballot paper is large, divided by a thick black line.
Above the line, you number at least six party or group boxes.
Below the line, you number at least twelve individual candidates.
These rules have applied since 2016.
Senators are elected by proportional representation using the single transferable vote.
At a normal half-Senate election, six senators are elected per state, and each needs a quota of about 14.
3 per cent of the votes.
Candidates who pass the quota have their surplus votes passed on at reduced value, and low candidates are excluded.
This helps smaller parties win seats in proportion to their support.
A fair and secret count.
Federal elections are run by the Australian Electoral Commission, an independent statutory authority established in 1984.
It keeps the electoral roll, counts the votes and regulates donation disclosure.
It also oversees redistributions, redrawing boundaries so seats in a state have roughly equal numbers of voters.
Independent committees, not politicians, draw them.
States and territories have their own commissions.
Before the 1850s, voting in Britain and its colonies was often public, which made bribery and intimidation easy.
In 1856 Victoria and South Australia introduced the secret ballot: official, government-printed papers listing all candidates, marked privately.
Britain adopted it in 1872.
American states took it up from the late 1880s and called it the 'Australian ballot'.
Making your vote count.
Australian citizens aged 18 and over must enrol, and 16 and 17 year olds can enrol early.
Enrol or update your address with the AEC, usually online, whenever you move.
Federal elections are held on a Saturday.
You can vote at any polling place in your state or territory, vote early at a pre-polling centre, or apply for a postal vote.
Polling places are often schools and halls, where sausage sizzles are a tradition.
Before election day, read about the candidates, not just the parties.
Follow the ballot instructions carefully, because a missing or repeated number can make a House vote informal.
How-to-vote cards are only suggestions; number the boxes however you choose.
Your vote is secret, and nobody can require you to reveal it.
The key idea: Voting in federal elections has been compulsory since 1924, and turnout is usually around 90 per cent.
Part two. Gerrymandering: winning by drawing the lines.
You can lose the popular vote and still win the election, if someone has drawn the map cleverly enough.
Meet the strange art of the gerrymander.
A salamander in Massachusetts.
In 1812 the Massachusetts legislature redrew its state senate districts to help the governing party, and Governor Elbridge Gerry signed the map into law.
One district north of Boston twisted so strangely that critics said it looked like a salamander.
The Boston Gazette published a cartoon turning it into a winged, clawed beast and named it the 'Gerry-mander'.
The insult stuck.
Gerry's name was pronounced with a hard G, like Gary, but the word is now almost always said with a soft G, like Jerry.
Gerry himself reportedly disliked the plan, yet his name is forever attached to it.
Packing and cracking.
Where each electorate elects one member, boundaries matter enormously.
Imagine a region with ten seats, where two parties each have half the voters.
Draw the lines one way and each party wins five seats.
Draw them another way and one party can win seven or eight.
There are two classic tricks.
Packing means cramming as many of your opponent's supporters as possible into a few seats, which they win by huge, wasteful margins.
Cracking means splitting the rest thinly across many seats, so they fall just short everywhere.
Their votes are not taken away.
They are arranged so that many make no difference.
With modern data and computers, these techniques can be applied with remarkable precision.
Unequal seats.
A cousin of the gerrymander is malapportionment, where some electorates hold many more voters than others.
If country seats have half the voters of city seats, each country vote counts roughly double.
It sometimes reflected a belief that rural areas needed extra representation, and sometimes it simply helped whoever drew the map.
Britain's 'rotten boroughs' were tiny constituencies with a handful of voters that still elected MPs, until reforms from 1832 began to sweep them away.
In South Australia, heavily weighted rural seats kept Thomas Playford's government in power for decades, a system nicknamed the Playmander.
Queensland's zonal system, introduced under Labor in 1949 and later reshaped by Country and National Party governments, was nicknamed the Bjelkemander after Premier Joh Bjelke-Petersen.
Both let parties win government with fewer votes than their rivals.
Drawing lines fairly.
After the Fitzgerald Inquiry into corruption in the late 1980s, Queensland moved to boundaries drawn by an independent commission with roughly equal enrolments.
Other states have also moved towards equal weighting over time.
Today federal boundaries are drawn by the Australian Electoral Commission, an independent statutory body, not by politicians.
When population shifts or a state's number of seats changes, a redistribution is held.
Committees propose boundaries, the public and parties can lodge objections, and an independent commission makes the final decision.
The law requires electorates in a state to have close to the same number of voters, within set tolerances, while also considering communities of interest, transport links and physical features.
States and territories run similar independent processes.
Parties still argue about decisions, but the pencil is out of the hands of those who benefit.
The fight elsewhere.
In the United States, district lines are usually drawn by state legislatures, so whichever party controls a state can shape its map.
Both major parties have been accused of gerrymandering where they hold power.
Some states have handed the job to independent or bipartisan commissions, often after citizen ballot initiatives.
US Supreme Court decisions in the 1960s, especially Reynolds v Sims in 1964, required state legislative districts to have roughly equal populations, a principle known as one person, one vote.
Courts also hear challenges over racial discrimination.
But in 2019, in Rucho v Common Cause, the Court held that partisan gerrymandering claims are political questions federal courts cannot resolve.
Researchers use measures such as the efficiency gap, which counts wasted votes, to detect unfair maps.
The key idea: The word 'gerrymander' comes from an 1812 cartoon mocking a district shaped like a monster.
Part three. Human rights: where they come from.
In 1948, after the horrors of the Second World War, the world's nations agreed on a list of rights belonging to every person.
Here's what's in it, and how Australia protects rights without a bill of rights.
Rights for every person.
Human rights are the basic freedoms that belong to every person, regardless of nationality, sex, race or religion.
The idea has deep roots.
Magna Carta limited a king's power in 1215, Enlightenment thinkers wrote of natural rights, and France in 1789 and the United States in 1791 put rights into law.
But the idea that rights apply to all humanity, as an international concern, took shape after 1945.
A UN commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt drafted a common standard.
Australia sat on the eight-country drafting committee, and H.
V. Evatt was President of the General Assembly when the Universal Declaration was adopted in Paris on 10 December 1948, by 48 votes to none with eight abstentions.
Its first article: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'
From declaration to treaties.
The Universal Declaration was not a treaty, so it didn't directly bind countries in law.
It was a statement of shared aims, though it has become enormously influential and has shaped many constitutions and laws.

To turn its principles into binding obligations, the UN adopted two major treaties in 1966: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
Together with the Declaration, they are often called the International Bill of Human Rights.
Other treaties followed on specific issues, including racial discrimination, discrimination against women, torture, children's rights and disability.
Two kinds of rights.
Civil and political rights mainly protect people from the misuse of state power and guarantee participation in public life.
They include the right to life, a fair trial, freedom of expression, religion and assembly, privacy, and the right to vote.
Many can be limited in certain circumstances, for example to protect public safety or the rights of others, but some, such as the ban on torture, are treated as absolute.
Economic, social and cultural rights cover fair work, joining a union, social security, adequate food and housing, health and education.
Because these depend on resources, countries must achieve them progressively.
Some argue they are as fundamental as civil rights, since freedom means little without food or schooling.
Others see them as policy goals for elected governments rather than rights for courts to enforce.
Australia's approach.
Australia is often described as the only Western democracy without a national bill or charter of rights.
Instead, rights are protected in several ways.
The Constitution contains a few express rights and an implied freedom of political communication.
The common law presumes Parliament doesn't intend to override basic freedoms unless it says so clearly.
Federal laws ban discrimination on grounds including race, 1975, sex, 1984, disability, 1992, and age, 2004, and the Australian Human Rights Commission handles complaints.
Since 2012, new federal bills must carry a statement on their compatibility with human rights, reviewed by a parliamentary committee.
The ACT, Victoria and Queensland have their own human rights Acts.
The debate, and your rights.
Supporters of a national bill of rights say current protections have gaps, that ordinary laws can be changed by any Parliament, and that a clear list would help vulnerable people.
Critics say elected Parliaments, not unelected judges, should balance rights, and that Australia already protects rights well.
A middle path is the Victorian model, where courts can declare laws inconsistent with rights but Parliament has the final say.
If you face discrimination at work, in housing, in education or from services, you can complain to the Australian Human Rights Commission or a state body.
In 1994, in Toonen v Australia, the UN Human Rights Committee found Tasmania's laws criminalising homosexual acts breached the right to privacy, and federal law changed soon after.
For advice on your situation, see a lawyer or community legal centre.
The key idea: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted on 10 December 1948, set out rights that belong to every person simply because they are human.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What does the law actually require of a voter at a federal election?
Answer. Attending and lodging a ballot paper.
Question two. What is a gerrymander?
Answer. Drawing electoral boundaries to favour one party.
Question three. What idea lies at the heart of the 1948 Universal Declaration?
Answer. Rights belong to every person simply because they are human.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
